subject: dermatology
title: Epidermal Layers and Architecture

steps.tx: **Epidermis** forms the stratified squamous, keratinized outer protective envelope of the human body, continuously renewing itself through orderly differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes. Averaging 0.1 millimetres in thickness over most body sites, it reaches up to 1.5 millimetres on friction-bearing surfaces like palms and soles. The tissue is completely avascular, relying entirely on passive diffusion of nutrients and oxygen from capillaries in the underlying papillary dermis across a continuous, semi-permeable basement membrane zone.
steps.say: The epidermis is a dynamic, self-renewing stratified squamous epithelium that lacks blood vessels entirely. It relies on passive nutrient diffusion from the vascular dermal papillae beneath the basement membrane.

steps.tx: **Stratum basale** constitutes the single germinative monolayer of columnar or cuboidal keratinocytes anchored directly to the basement membrane through specialized hemidesmosomes and type XVII collagen. These proliferative stem cells express keratin 5 and keratin 14 intermediate filaments. Interspersed among basal keratinocytes are dendrite-bearing melanocytes, which synthesize melanin pigments and transfer melanosomes to approximately thirty-six neighboring keratinocytes, as well as neuroendocrine Merkel cells that function as slow-adapting mechanoreceptors.
steps.say: The basal stratum is a single proliferative layer producing keratins 5 and 14. Melanocytes reside here, transferring pigment to thirty-six keratinocytes, alongside tactile Merkel cells that detect mechanical touch.

steps.tx: Read this clinical view from surface to base before naming any lesion. The **stratum basale** sits deepest as one row of dividing keratinocytes on the basement membrane, and every cell above it is an older keratinocyte flattening as it climbs. Spinous cells link by desmosomes, granular cells gather keratohyalin, and the cornified sheet finally sheds. A disease can be placed by asking which of these layers has thickened, split or vanished.
steps.say: Skin disease can be located by layer: basal division below, spinous links, granular change and a shedding cornified surface above. Ask which layer is thickened, split or lost.

vis.alt: Clinical style layered view of epidermis from stratum basale to cornified surface, each layer labelled.
vis.caption: Epidermal layers are stacked from the basal germinative row up to the shedding cornified surface. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Stratum spinosum** consists of five to ten layers of polyhedral keratinocytes that synthesize differentiation-specific keratins 1 and 10. In histological preparations, cellular dehydration creates microscopic spiny intercellular bridges, which represent intact desmosomal plaques anchoring adjacent cells. Scattered within this suprabasal layer are bone marrow-derived dendritic Langerhans cells containing tennis-racket-shaped Birbeck granules, which capture epidermal protein antigens and migrate to regional lymph nodes to prime naive helper T lymphocytes.
steps.say: The spinous stratum contains plump polygonal keratinocytes rich in desmosomes. Antigen-presenting Langerhans cells containing Birbeck granules patrol this layer, capturing antigens and traveling to regional lymph nodes.

steps.tx: **Stratum granulosum** comprises two to four layers of flattened, diamond-shaped keratinocytes containing dense, deeply basophilic keratohyalin granules. These granules contain high concentrations of profilaggrin and loricrin, essential for assembling the tough cornified cell envelope. Simultaneously, lamellar bodies (Odland bodies) within these cells synthesize ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, extruding them into the extracellular space to form the primary impermeable lipid seal that prevents transepidermal water loss.
steps.say: The granular layer produces basophilic keratohyalin granules rich in profilaggrin and loricrin. Membrane-coating Odland bodies release lipid mixtures into intercellular spaces, establishing the skin vital waterproof barrier.

right.title: Lamellar (Odland) Bodies
points: Rich in ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids

steps.tx: **Stratum lucidum** is a thin, clear, highly refractile, eosinophilic transitional layer situated immediately superficial to the stratum granulosum. It is present exclusively in the thick, hairless skin of the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Cells in this layer are flattened, dead, and have lost their nuclei and cytoplasmic organelles, with their interiors densely packed with eleidin, a semi-fluid protein transformation product of keratohyalin.
steps.say: The stratum lucidum is an anucleate, clear band found solely on friction-bearing thick skin like palms and soles. Its cells are packed with eleidin, acting as a flexible buffer beneath the thick palmar stratum corneum.

vis.title: Architectural Differences Between Thick and Thin Skin

steps.tx: **Stratum corneum** constitutes the final physical barrier of the skin, configured in a classic brick-and-mortar architecture. Anucleate, flattened, polygonal cornified squames (corneocytes) function as the protein bricks, composed of densely aggregated keratin macrofibrils enveloped by an insoluble cross-linked protein shell. The surrounding mortar consists of organized multilamellar lipid sheets containing ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids. This barrier prevents passive desiccation, resists physical shear stresses, and blocks microbial invasion.
steps.say: The stratum corneum is built like a brick wall: flattened protein corneocytes are the bricks, while intercellular lipid lamellae act as the mortar. This structure provides our main defense against water loss and environmental microbes.

steps.tx: **Epidermal transit time** represents the total duration required for a newly divided basal keratinocyte to differentiate, migrate through the spinous and granular strata, cornify, and desquamate from the skin surface. Under normal physiological conditions, transit takes approximately twenty-eight days: fourteen days from basal layer to stratum corneum, and fourteen days within the cornified layer. In hyperproliferative diseases like psoriasis, this transit is accelerated to four days, preventing complete cell maturation.
steps.say: A basal keratinocyte normally takes twenty-eight days to migrate upward and shed from the surface: fourteen days through viable layers and fourteen days through the corneum. Psoriasis slashes this time to four days.

steps.tx: **Parakeratosis** is the pathological retention of intact pyknotic nuclei within the stratum corneum, signalling severely accelerated epidermal proliferation and defective keratinization. Normally, keratinocyte nuclei and cytoplasmic organelles are enzymatically degraded during the granular-to-corneal transition. In conditions such as psoriasis and subacute eczema, rapid cell transit skips this degradation step, causing parakeratotic scaling accompanied by complete disappearance of the underlying stratum granulosum.
steps.say: Parakeratosis is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum due to abnormally fast epidermal transit. Because cells reach the surface prematurely, the granular layer vanishes and scales flake off easily.
